title: The Gene's Eye and the Second Replicator: Nairobi to College Station
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Nairobi, born in the war year
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the hospital is named in no reachable source
stops.campa: Clinton Richard Dawkins is born in Nairobi on the twenty-sixth of March, in the second full year of the war, to Clinton John Dawkins and Jean Mary Vyvyan Dawkins. The father is a colonial agricultural officer who has been called up into the King's African Rifles, so the son arrives into a household run on postings and the Latin names of plants. Which hospital took the mother in is recorded nowhere a reader can check. Kenya is British, and the Italians are being driven out of Abyssinia to the north. The family stays in East Africa. He will not see England until he is eight years old.
sources: EBSCO Research Starters, biography of Richard Dawkins
suggested_refs: Colonial Agricultural Service and King's African Rifles service records for Clinton John Dawkins

stops.name: Thyolo, the Nyasaland years
stops.date_confidence: year of the posting attested by his own account; month not recorded
stops.campa: In 1943 the father is posted back to Nyasaland, and the family settles in the Cholo hills among tea estates and red laterite roads. Here the boy is two, and then six, and then eight, and the natural world is not a school subject but the whole of the outdoors: chameleons on a fence, frangipani after rain, a mother who names plants accurately when asked. He is taken to the Anglican service and believes what he is told there, in the ordinary way of a small child. It is the only country he has lived in. The African years run to 1949.
sources: Richard Dawkins, 'Growing Up in Ethology', Edge.org
Obituary of John Dawkins, Boing Boing (2010)
suggested_refs: An Appetite for Wonder (2013), the Nyasaland chapters

stops.name: Over Norton Park, the inherited acres
stops.date_confidence: relocation year attested; the telegram and its date are contested between accounts and are not resolved here
stops.campa: A kinsman dies and two hundred and ten acres of Oxfordshire fall to the father, land the Dawkinses have held since James Dawkins bought it in 1726. The family comes home to a country the boy has never lived in: cold, rationed, green, with a farm to be learned from the ground upward. Whether the news came by telegram, and whether it came in 1946 or in 1949, the accounts do not agree and no document reachable now settles it. The relocation year itself is not in doubt. In 1949 a colonial agricultural officer becomes an English farmer.
sources: Oxfordshire History Centre, catalogue of Dawkins family papers
suggested_refs: The 1726 purchase of Over Norton by James Dawkins
An Appetite for Wonder (2013), on the inheritance

stops.name: Chafyn Grove, the first English school
stops.date_confidence: year attested; term of entry inferred from the school calendar
stops.campa: On the edge of Salisbury he is put into a small preparatory boarding school, his first sustained schooling in England. He is eight, brought in from another continent, and has to learn the grammar of an English institution: bells, dormitories, chapel twice on Sunday, the exact tone in which a boy addresses a master. Religion here is not questioned, it is timetabled. He is a competent and unremarkable pupil who likes machines and small animals. Nothing any master at Chafyn Grove wrote down about him has been kept, or at least none of it is reachable now.
suggested_refs: Chafyn Grove School registers, 1949-1954

stops.name: Oundle, Laundimer House
stops.date_confidence: years 1954 to 1959 attested; the month is inferred from the school year
stops.campa: He goes on to Oundle, an Anglican public school in Northamptonshire kept by the Grocers' Company, and is housed in Laundimer. Chapel is compulsory and daily; the school also teaches its boys to take an argument apart and put it back together. He reads, dissects, keeps beetles, and takes the sciences more seriously than the classics. The chapel and the debating habit run side by side for five years without anybody at the school remarking on the arrangement. He is there from 1954 to 1959, and sits through chapel every morning of it.
sources: Richard Dawkins, An Appetite for Wonder (2013)
suggested_refs: Laundimer House records, Oundle School

stops.name: Oundle, the argument from design gives way
stops.date_confidence: traditional: dated by his own memoir to about the age of sixteen, with no month or day recorded
stops.campa: At about sixteen he stops believing. By his own later account it is not rebellion and not grievance but a piece of reasoning: the argument from design was the last thing holding the belief up, and once he understands that natural selection produces the appearance of design with nobody designing, there is nothing under it. What no sermon in that chapel had shaken, Charles Darwin's argument removes. He tells nobody in particular. Chapel is compulsory, so the bell rings at the same hour and he goes to it as before.
sources: Richard Dawkins, An Appetite for Wonder (2013)
suggested_refs: William Paley, Natural Theology (1802), the argument he is losing here and will answer at length in 1986

stops.name: Balliol College, reading zoology
stops.date_confidence: matriculation year attested; term inferred from the university calendar
stops.campa: He comes up to Balliol to read zoology, an undergraduate with a farmer's hands and an African childhood behind him. Oxford zoology in these years is pulled between the dissecting bench and the new study of behaviour, and the teaching is by tutorial, which means defending a position weekly, in a room, to a man who has read more than you have and will interrupt. Nothing in the college record marks him out among his year, and no tutor's report on him is reachable in any archive. He takes a second-class degree in 1962.
suggested_refs: Balliol College matriculation registers, 1959

stops.name: The Department of Zoology, apprenticed to Tinbergen
stops.date_confidence: year attested; term inferred
stops.campa: He stays on for a doctorate under Nikolaas Tinbergen, who will share a Nobel Prize for the study of animal behaviour and who trains his students to ask what a behaviour is for. Dawkins builds models of how a chick decides between pecking and not pecking, and writes some of the earliest behavioural software in the department. The animal starts to look to him like a device running a program, and the program like something that could be written down exactly. He is punching the cards himself, one line of instruction to a card, for a machine that fills a room.
sources: Richard Dawkins, 'Growing Up in Ethology', Edge.org
suggested_refs: Nikolaas Tinbergen, 'On Aims and Methods of Ethology' (1963)

stops.name: The Department of Zoology, the doctorate and the assistant year
stops.date_confidence: DPhil completed in 1966; month not recorded
stops.campa: The doctorate is finished in 1966, on decision-making in animal behaviour, and he stays a further year as Tinbergen's research assistant, lecturing in the master's place when the master is away. Around him the ethologists argue about instinct and drive, and use the phrase for the good of the species freely, in seminars and in print, as though somebody had once sat down and checked whether selection could work that way at all. He begins to suspect nobody has. He is twenty-five.
suggested_refs: W. D. Hamilton, 'The Genetical Evolution of Social Behaviour' (1964), the paper the objection eventually rests on

stops.name: Annestown, the marriage above the Waterford cliffs
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; a common secondary account placing the wedding in England is contradicted by the Annestown record
stops.campa: On the nineteenth of August he marries the ethologist Marian Stamp in the Protestant church at Annestown, on the Waterford coast. They met in the Oxford department. Both will spend their working lives on animal behaviour, and she will be elected to the Royal Society in her own right and become the authority on what an animal's welfare actually consists of. The marriage will last seventeen years and end in divorce in 1984. Within weeks of the wedding the pair are in California.
sources: Biographical summaries of Marian Stamp Dawkins (Wikidata and derived sources)
suggested_refs: Marian Stamp Dawkins, Animal Suffering (1980)

stops.name: Berkeley, an assistant professor in a year of marches
stops.date_confidence: appointment 1967 to 1969 attested; the month is inferred from the academic year
stops.campa: He takes an assistant professorship in zoology at Berkeley and arrives on the loudest campus in America. He teaches animal behaviour by day. By his own much later telling he is drawn into the demonstrations against the Vietnam War going on around him; no contemporary record of his part in them has been found, and the detail rests entirely on retrospect, told decades after the fact and by the man himself. Two California years, and then Oxford writes offering a lectureship. He takes it.
suggested_refs: University of California, Berkeley, Department of Zoology appointment records 1967-1969

stops.name: New College, the fellowship
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month not recorded
stops.campa: He returns to Oxford as a lecturer in zoology and a fellow of New College, and he will hold that fellowship, tutorial and then emeritus, for the rest of his life. It gives him rooms, a dining table with historians and lawyers along it, and pupils to be argued with weekly. In the winter of 1973 the miners' strike cuts the power and stops the laboratory work, and with the electricity off he begins writing a book for the general reader about what a gene actually is. The strike ends. The manuscript does not.
suggested_refs: Brief Candle in the Dark (2015), on the writing of The Selfish Gene during the power cuts

stops.name: Oxford, the university press publishes
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: Oxford University Press publishes The Selfish Gene on the twenty-eighth of October, two hundred and twenty-four pages, written for anybody who can read. Its argument is that what natural selection acts on is neither the species nor the group nor even the individual animal, but the gene, and that bodies are vehicles built by genes to carry themselves into the next round. Reviewers take the title for cynicism about human beings; he insists it is arithmetic about molecules. The book has never since been out of print.
stops.quote: We are survival machines—robot vehicles blindly programmed to preserve the selfish molecules known as genes. This is a truth which still fills me with astonishment.
stops.quote_source: The Selfish Gene (1976), Preface to the first edition
sources: Text of the Preface as reproduced at publicism.info
suggested_refs: Robert Trivers's foreword to the 1976 first edition

stops.name: Oxford, chapter eleven and the second replicator
stops.date_confidence: attested; the chapter closes the first edition
stops.campa: The last chapter of the first edition is written almost as an afterthought and outlives everything around it. Having spent ten chapters on one replicator, he proposes that a second is already loose on this planet: a unit of cultural transmission that copies itself from brain to brain by imitation. He wants a monosyllable that sounds like gene, cuts the Greek mimeme down to size, and gets meme, to rhyme with cream. Tunes, catchphrases, clothes fashions, ways of building arches.
stops.quote: Just as genes propagate themselves in the gene pool by leaping from body to body via sperms or eggs, so memes propagate themselves in the meme pool by leaping from brain to brain via a process which, in the broad sense, can be called imitation.
stops.quote_source: The Selfish Gene (1976), ch. 11, 'Memes: the new replicators'
sources: The Selfish Gene (1976), ch. 11, text as reproduced at publicism.info
suggested_refs: William S. Burroughs, The Ticket That Exploded (1962), 'the word is now a virus', read alongside the meme by later scholarship (Oliver Harris)

stops.name: Oxford, the phenotype carried past the skin
stops.date_confidence: publication year attested; month not recorded
stops.campa: The Extended Phenotype pushes the argument out of the body. A beaver's dam, a caddis larva's case of grit, the altered behaviour of a snail carrying a parasite: all of these are effects of genes, and the skin is not a boundary that selection respects. The gene's-eye view now has a research programme attached, and a long public quarrel with Stephen Jay Gould, who reads the same evidence and does not reach the same conclusion. Dawkins calls it the one book of his written for professionals, and the one he would rescue from a fire.
stops.quote: I find his reasoning wrong but interesting, which, incidentally, he has been kind enough to tell me, is how he usually finds mine.
stops.quote_source: Footnote on Stephen Jay Gould added in the 1989 second edition of The Selfish Gene; quoted through secondary academic accounts of the dispute
sources: Secondary academic literature on the Dawkins-Gould dispute
suggested_refs: Stephen Jay Gould and Richard Lewontin, 'The Spandrels of San Marco' (1979)

stops.name: Oxford, the watchmaker who cannot see ahead
stops.date_confidence: publication year attested; month not recorded
stops.campa: The Blind Watchmaker takes up William Paley's watch found lying on a heath and answers it a hundred and eighty years late. Paley reasoned from a mechanism back to a maker. Dawkins sets out how cumulative selection, small changes kept and compounded across depths of time no one can picture, builds mechanism with nobody choosing anything. To make the accumulation visible he writes a program that breeds branching shapes on a screen, biomorphs, so that a reader can watch the process do its work in an afternoon at a keyboard.
stops.quote: Natural selection is the blind watchmaker, blind because it does not see ahead, does not plan consequences, has no purpose in view.
stops.quote_source: The Blind Watchmaker (1986); quoted through secondary sources, not verified against a primary edition
suggested_refs: William Paley, Natural Theology (1802)
The biomorph program distributed with the 1986 Blind Watchmaker software

stops.name: The Oxford Union, against the creationists
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the exact date of the debate is not recorded in reachable sources
stops.campa: In the chamber off Cornmarket Street he takes the evolution side with John Maynard Smith against A. E. Wilder-Smith and Edgar Andrews, who argue that the living world was designed. It is a Union motion, decided by undergraduates walking through one door or the other, and the creationist side is beaten heavily. He is forty-five, and it is the first time he has argued biology to a hall that votes. No reachable record gives the day within 1986, or the count on the division.
suggested_refs: Oxford Union debate records, 1986

stops.name: Los Angeles, a prize for a book about design
stops.date_confidence: award year attested; the ceremony venue is not named in reachable sources
stops.campa: The Blind Watchmaker takes the Los Angeles Times Book Prize, in a country where the argument the book answers is refought every year in front of elected school boards. An English zoologist's quarrel with an eighteenth-century archdeacon turns out not to be a historical curiosity in the United States. No source consulted names the room in Los Angeles where the prize was handed over, only the year. In Britain the same book takes the Royal Society of Literature award.
suggested_refs: Los Angeles Times Book Prize records, 1987

stops.name: Carlton House Terrace, the Faraday Award
stops.date_confidence: award year attested; month not recorded
stops.campa: The Royal Society gives him the Michael Faraday Prize for the communication of science, a year after the Zoological Society of London gave him its silver medal. Oxford makes him a Reader in zoology in the same year. The honours are all for the thing he had not set out to become: the explainer, the man who can get natural selection into a paragraph that a stranger finishes. No source names the room the Zoological Society handed its medal over in the year before. He is forty-nine.
suggested_refs: Royal Society, Michael Faraday Prize citation, 1990

stops.name: The Royal Institution, Growing Up in the Universe
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the lectures are traditionally delivered over the Christmas period
stops.campa: In the theatre on Albemarle Street he gives the Royal Institution Christmas Lectures, five of them, to a hall of children and a television audience beyond it. He brings on a model eye, a real skull, a computer breeding shapes, a tank of water; he asks what it is to grow up inside a universe that was not made with anyone in mind and is older than any story about it. The series is called Growing Up in the Universe. It is broadcast and taped, and the tapes go into schoolrooms for a generation after.
suggested_refs: Growing Up in the Universe, Royal Institution Christmas Lectures 1991, broadcast recordings

stops.name: Conway Hall, the Voltaire Lecture
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the essay was drafted in 1991 and published in 1993
stops.campa: On the sixth of November he delivers the Voltaire Lecture in Red Lion Square and takes the meme out of the seminar room to point it at religion. Faith, he argues, spreads through minds by the mechanisms of a virus: trust, repetition, infection early enough that the host is in no position to examine it. It is the first time he argues in public and under his own name that belief is a thing to be explained rather than an opinion to be deferred to. The text appears the following year in Bo Dahlbom's collection of essays on Daniel Dennett.
stops.quote: When you plant a fertile meme in my mind you literally parasitize my brain, turning it into a vehicle for the meme's propagation in just the way that a virus may parasitize the genetic mechanism of a host cell.
stops.quote_source: The Selfish Gene (1976), ch. 11, the passage the 1992 lecture extends
sources: Bo Dahlbom (ed.), Dennett and His Critics: Demystifying Mind (Blackwell, 1993)
suggested_refs: Richard Dawkins, 'Viruses of the Mind' (1993)

stops.name: Oxford, a chair endowed for one man
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month not recorded
stops.campa: Charles Simonyi, who wrote the word processor that made him rich, endows a professorship at Oxford for the public understanding of science and names Dawkins its first holder. He is fifty-four. The chair carries no undergraduate teaching and one duty: to explain science to people who are not scientists, at whatever length that takes. Whether the man holding it is still a zoologist or has become a writer with a laboratory behind him is a question the deed of endowment does not settle.
stops.quote: The universe we observe has precisely the properties we should expect if there is, at bottom, no design, no purpose, no evil and no good, nothing but blind pitiless indifference.
stops.quote_source: River Out of Eden (1995); quoted through secondary sources, not verified against a primary edition
sources: Wikipedia, 'Simonyi Professor for the Public Understanding of Science'
suggested_refs: The deed of endowment of the Charles Simonyi Professorship, 1995

stops.name: Osaka, the Cosmos Prize
stops.date_confidence: award year attested; month not recorded
stops.campa: A Japanese foundation gives him the International Cosmos Prize, awarded for work that illuminates how living things belong to one another. In the same year the Royal Society of Literature elects him a fellow, for the prose. Two honours in one twelvemonth: one for a vision of life, one for English sentences. He is fifty-six, and the Cosmos citation is for a body of work rather than for any single finding. No reachable source records the room either prize was handed over in, or whether he was present to take them.
suggested_refs: International Cosmos Prize citation, 1997

stops.name: Carlton House Terrace, elected to the Royal Society
stops.date_confidence: election year attested; month not recorded
stops.campa: He is elected a Fellow of the Royal Society at sixty. The election is argued over in the corridors beforehand: he has published less primary research than most candidates and more books than all of them together, and the case for him rests on the theoretical argument of The Extended Phenotype as much as on any experiment he ever ran. Then he signs the charter book that fellows have signed since the seventeenth century, on a fresh line under the names of everybody admitted before him.
suggested_refs: Royal Society election certificate for Richard Dawkins, 2001

stops.name: Monterey, militant atheism from a conference stage
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month not recorded, and the conference was then held annually at Monterey
stops.campa: At the conference in Monterey he gives a short talk under a blunt title, Militant atheism, and asks the American unbelievers in the room to stop being quiet: to say so, to organize, to stop treating the question as one of manners. The hall is full of engineers and investors, and the talk runs eighteen minutes. The recording goes onto the internet and travels further than any lecture he has given from a podium. The book that makes the same argument at length is four years away.
suggested_refs: TED 2002 conference programme

stops.name: The Galapagos, the pilgrimage to the islands
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: one account dates the visit to a 2005 pilgrimage, another attaches it to the 2008 Channel 4 filming, and the two cannot be reconciled from reachable sources
stops.campa: He crosses to the archipelago on the equator: the finches, the tortoises, the black lava, the islands where Charles Darwin gathered specimens that would not sort themselves into the order he had expected. Dawkins has spent thirty years arguing Darwin's case in a vocabulary Darwin never had, of genes, copying errors, and information. The sources disagree about which year he made the crossing and for which production. That he stood on the islands themselves is not disputed by any of them.
suggested_refs: charles_darwin.journey.json, the Beagle's Galapagos landfall of 1835
The Ancestor's Tale (2004)

stops.name: Hamburg, the Shakespeare Prize
stops.date_confidence: award year attested; month not recorded
stops.campa: The Alfred Toepfer Foundation awards him its Shakespeare Prize in Hamburg, a German honour for English-language cultural achievement usually given to novelists, dramatists, and directors. This year it goes to a man who writes about beetles, bats, and the arithmetic of kinship, and the committee is judging the prose rather than the biology in it. What hall the ceremony was held in, and what he said there, are recorded in no source reachable now. He is sixty-four.
suggested_refs: Alfred Toepfer Foundation, Shakespeare Prize records, 2005

stops.name: Oxford, The God Delusion
stops.date_confidence: publication year attested; month not recorded
stops.campa: The God Delusion is published and sells in the millions across a dozen languages. It states the God Hypothesis as a claim about what exists, insists that such a claim is a scientific question and not a private consolation immune from examination, and answers it no. He has been a public explainer for thirty years; from this book onward he is read as a combatant, and the post arrives accordingly. In the same year he founds a foundation for reason and science carrying his own name.
stops.quote: Instead I shall define the God Hypothesis more defensibly: there exists a superhuman, supernatural intelligence who deliberately designed and created the universe and everything in it, including us.
stops.quote_source: The God Delusion (2006), ch. 2, 'The God Hypothesis'
suggested_refs: Alister McGrath, The Dawkins Delusion? (2007)

stops.name: Frankfurt, the Deschner Prize
stops.date_confidence: award year attested; month not recorded
stops.campa: He receives the Deschner Prize, named for Karlheinz Deschner, who spent a working life compiling a criminal history of Christianity volume by volume in German. The award comes a year after The God Delusion, out of a continental tradition of anticlerical writing far older and considerably angrier than the English one he belongs to. Deschner had been at that history for twenty years by then and would not finish it for another six. It is a lineage Dawkins did not pick and does not decline. The prize is handed over in Frankfurt and he accepts it.
suggested_refs: Karlheinz Deschner, Kriminalgeschichte des Christentums (1986-2013)

segments.name: The Four Horsemen and the Debating Years

stops.name: Washington, four men and a camera
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: On the thirtieth of September he sits down with Christopher Hitchens, Daniel Dennett, and Sam Harris for two hours of unmoderated talk about religion, civility, and what a person may say aloud in a country founded on saying things aloud. There is no audience and no motion to vote on. The recording is released as The Four Horsemen, a name none of the four chose for themselves. The camera stands in a private room on a tripod, running from the first minute to the last.
suggested_refs: The Four Horsemen: The Conversation That Sparked an Atheist Revolution (2019 book edition)

stops.name: Birmingham, Alabama, against John Lennox
stops.date_confidence: month and year attested; the day is not recorded in reachable sources
stops.campa: In Alabama, hosted by a Christian foundation, he debates John Lennox, an Oxford mathematician who is his colleague at home and his opponent on this platform. The question is whether The God Delusion has buried God. Lennox is unruffled, Northern Irish, and professionally at ease with proof; Dawkins is the more famous man in the hall and the less comfortable one in it. The exchange is filmed and watched by more people than either has lectured to in a lifetime. They will do it again in Oxford the next autumn.
sources: bethinking.org, 'The John Lennox - Richard Dawkins Debate'
suggested_refs: John Lennox, God's Undertaker: Has Science Buried God? (2007)

stops.name: Oxford, the chair given up
stops.date_confidence: retirement in September 2008 attested; the exact day follows the academic year
stops.campa: He retires from the Simonyi chair at the end of September, thirteen years after it was endowed for him, and it passes to the mathematician Marcus du Sautoy. He stays an emeritus fellow of New College, the college he first entered as a young lecturer in 1970. The formal university career closes at sixty-seven, forty-nine years after he first matriculated a quarter of a mile away at Balliol. He keeps the rooms and the college dinners and the title emeritus. What he gives up is the obligation to be in Oxford at all.
suggested_refs: Marcus du Sautoy's inaugural Simonyi lecture, 2009

stops.name: The Oxford University Museum, Has Science Buried God?
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: Under the iron and glass of the museum where the famous Victorian quarrel over apes and ancestry was held, he meets Lennox a second time, the motion put as a question: has science buried God? The debate is filmed and put online, and cut afterwards into clips by supporters of both men, each clip ending where their own man is ahead. Around the two of them the cast-iron columns are carved with leaves copied from living plants, and the dinosaurs stand where the Victorians set them down.
sources: bethinking.org, 'The John Lennox - Richard Dawkins Debate'
Independent Catholic News, 'Oxford: Richard Dawkins in debate with John Lennox'
suggested_refs: Recording of 'Has Science Buried God?', Oxford University Museum of Natural History, 21 October 2008

stops.name: London, the buses
stops.date_confidence: campaign launch attested to January 2009; Dawkins pledged matching funds in October 2008
stops.campa: Eight hundred buses go into service in Britain carrying an advertisement he half paid for, after a journalist asked in print why only religious slogans ever appeared on the sides of them. He had pledged matching funds in October; the target was met in four days and passed many times over. The word probably sits in the text because the advertising code requires that a claim be capable of substantiation. It is the word that gets argued about most. Believers object to the sentence, unbelievers object to the hedge, and the buses run their routes through the January dark either way.
stops.quote: There's probably no God. Now stop worrying and enjoy your life.
stops.quote_source: Atheist Bus Campaign slogan, British buses, January 2009
suggested_refs: Ariane Sherine's original Guardian column proposing the campaign (2008)

stops.name: La Jolla, the Nierenberg Prize
stops.date_confidence: award year attested; month not recorded
stops.campa: The Scripps Institution of Oceanography gives him the Nierenberg Prize for science in the public interest, at a laboratory on a Pacific cliff devoted to an ocean he has never worked on. The citation is for the public interest, not for oceanography: the award is for transmission rather than for research. He lectures at Scripps and goes home to Oxford. His book assembling the physical evidence for evolution, written for people who accept none of it, belongs to the same year.
suggested_refs: Nierenberg Prize citation, Scripps Institution of Oceanography, 2009

stops.name: The Cooper Union, the greatest show
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the surviving photograph of this appearance is captioned 2010; an earlier reading of the same source dated it 2006, which does not fit the book
stops.campa: He speaks in the Great Hall of the Cooper Union in Manhattan, the brick basement room where nineteenth-century New York went to hear its arguments settled. The subject is The Greatest Show on Earth, his assembly of the physical evidence for evolution: fossils in their strata, ring species, molecular clocks, bacteria bred through fifty thousand generations in a laboratory flask. Outside the hall a large share of the country rejects the conclusion. The year of the appearance is not firm: a surviving photograph is captioned 2010, and an earlier reading of the same source gave 2006.
suggested_refs: The Greatest Show on Earth: The Evidence for Evolution (2009)

stops.name: Bedford Square, a private college
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month not recorded
stops.campa: He joins the founding professoriate of the New College of the Humanities in Bloomsbury, a private undergraduate college charging fees at twice the public rate, announced by the philosopher A. C. Grayling with a roster of famous names attached. Dawkins is seventy, and lectures there on evolutionary biology, inside a humanities college, with an Oxford emeritus fellowship still behind him. From the first week the place is attacked as a shop for the children of the rich.
suggested_refs: New College of the Humanities founding prospectus, 2011

stops.name: Oxford, a book for readers of twelve
stops.date_confidence: publication year attested; month not recorded
stops.campa: The Magic of Reality is written for readers of about twelve and illustrated throughout by Dave McKean. Every chapter opens with the stories people have told about a thing, the sun, an earthquake, the first man and the first woman, and then sets down what is actually known and how anybody came to know it. The myths are told straight, at length and without mockery, before the evidence is laid beside them. The reader is left to compare the two accounts unaided. It is the first book he has written for the age he was himself at Chafyn Grove.
suggested_refs: Dave McKean's illustrations for The Magic of Reality (2011)

stops.name: London, the word taken out of his hands
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the filming location of the video installation is not named in reachable sources
stops.campa: Filmed for a video installation, he is asked about internet memes and says the internet has hijacked the term. His memes mutated by copying error and were selected blindly across generations, in the way genes are; the captioned pictures mutate because a person sits down and alters them on purpose. It is a distinction he holds to and almost nobody using the word observes. The word is thirty-seven years old by now. He sets the distinction out again whenever anyone puts the question to him, and has been doing so for years.
stops.quote: An internet meme is a hijacking of the original idea.
stops.quote_source: Richard Dawkins, in the Marshmallow Laser Feast video 'Just for Hits' (2013)
suggested_refs: The OED's separate first citation for the internet sense of meme, a CNN broadcast of 24 January 1998

stops.name: Oxford, the memoirs and the timeline
stops.date_confidence: publication years 2013 and 2015 attested; months not recorded
stops.campa: An Appetite for Wonder carries him from Nairobi to the writing of The Selfish Gene; Brief Candle in the Dark, two years later, takes up everything that came after it. He writes the childhood without nostalgia and the quarrels without much retreat. In the same period his Twitter account produces sentences that occupy the newspapers for weeks. One of them sets the Nobel count of the world's Muslims against that of a single Cambridge college. Whether the man writing the memoirs and the man writing the timeline can be read as one person is a question the two bodies of text leave open.
stops.quote: I think that a new kind of replicator has recently emerged on this very planet. It is staring us in the face. It is still in its infancy, still drifting clumsily about in its primeval soup, but already it is achieving evolutionary change at a rate that leaves the old gene panting far behind.
stops.quote_source: The Selfish Gene (1976), ch. 11; quoted through secondary sources, not fetched verbatim from a primary edition
suggested_refs: Press coverage of the 2013 Trinity College Nobel tweet

stops.name: The John Radcliffe Hospital, the stroke
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: Alone at home he notices that his left arm is not behaving properly, and is taken to the stroke unit on Headley Way. It is a haemorrhagic stroke; it takes coordination and leaves speech and memory where they were. He is discharged after four days and records a message thanking those who wrote to him, including, he notes, the ones who wrote to say they had prayed. A tour of Australia and New Zealand due to open at the end of the month is cancelled while he is still in Oxford.

stops.name: Oxford, the award taken back
stops.date_confidence: board decision attested to the day; the April tweet is dated to the month
stops.campa: In April he posts a message setting the case of Rachel Dolezal beside that of transgender people and adding that he does not intend to disparage anyone, which slows the response not at all. On the twentieth the board of the American Humanist Association withdraws the Humanist of the Year award it gave him in 1996, twenty-five years after handing it over. Steven Pinker and Rebecca Newberger Goldstein object in public to a body revoking an honour over opinions. He marries Jana Lenzova the same year.
sources: American Humanist Association board statement, 20 April 2021
Why Evolution Is True, Pinker and Goldstein response

stops.name: Oxford, the last argument
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month not recorded
stops.campa: He writes an opinion piece with the physicist Alan Sokal against the phrase sex assigned at birth, arguing that sex in mammals is observed at birth and not assigned by anyone, and that clinical language has bent under social pressure rather than evidence. Sokal is the man who in 1996 placed a deliberately meaningless paper in a cultural studies journal to make a point about rigour. The two are fighting the same war they fought in the nineties, on ground that has moved. Dawkins announces a farewell speaking tour for the autumn.
suggested_refs: Alan Sokal, 'Transgressing the Boundaries' (1996) and the Social Text affair

stops.name: College Station, the Trotter Prize
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: On the thirteenth of February he shares the Trotter Prize with the computer scientist Rosalind Picard and lectures in Rudder Auditorium at Texas A&M, an award founded for work on information, complexity, and inference, in a state whose school boards have fought over the teaching of evolution for the whole of his working life. He is eighty-three. Forty-nine years earlier, in a chapter written as an afterthought, he proposed that ideas copy themselves from head to head; the hall is full of people who knew the word before they knew his name.
sources: Texas A&M University events listing, February 2025
